To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

fibrinogen molecules polymerize by a two‐stage process, first to staggered overlapped fibrillar oligomers by end‐to‐side peptide A release, and second to end‐to‐ligated fibrils by end‐toend peptide A ligation.

(1) the first A peptide is released from the N‐terminal end of the molecule by thrombin more slowly than the second, by a factor of 16; (2) oligomer assembly follows the statistics of polycondensation, and (3) the staggered overlap is the most stable conformation of fibrin oligomer.

the kinetics of fibrin polymerization can be described quantitatively by a theory that assumes that the rate constants for release of the first and second A peptides are in the ratio q = 16 and that the assembly of ligated oligomer chains follows the statistics of a linear polycondensation with both difunctional (A‐peptide‐releasing) and monofunctionnal (B‐peptide‐forming) combining units.

the kinetics of fibrin polymerization.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rate of ligation of fibrin is determined by the rate of peptide A release by thrombin, and the rate of assembly is determined by the concentration of fibrinoligated fibrin.
the kinetics of the initial stages of fibrin assembly is controlled by the rates of release of the A peptides, the rates of ligation of these, and the rate of assembly of the oligomers.
, under the experimental conditions of these studies, the rate‐determining step is peptide A release, and the subsequent assembly and ligation of oligomers are rapid.

fibrin polymerization is a two‐stage process: first, the release and ligation of peptide A, and second, the assembly of the ligated monomers into staggered overlappd oligomers, which are subsequently split to form the end‐to‐ end ligated fibrin strands.

, for thrombin concentration less than 0.013 units per milliliter and fibrinoligation activity greater than 30 mg of fibrinoligation protein per liter, the theory of this paper describes the kinetics of fibrin polymerization in the presence of calcium ion and fibrinoligated activity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, under physiological conditions, the kinetics of fibrin polymerization are dominated by the rapid release of A peptides and the slower ligation of the γ‐chains of the fibrin monomer.
the size of the fibrin oligomers is determined by the relative rates of peptide release and ligation, and that the latter is a rate limiting step.
fibrin polymerization is a complex process, involving several steps, each of which may be rate determining under different experimental conditions.
